title: Bài 8: Cầu Nguyện Và Thờ Phượng
subtitle: Prayer & Worship — Psalm 95 (come, let us worship and bow down); John 4:19-26 (worship in spirit and truth) · Ngữ pháp: Modals — advice (should / ought to), obligation (must / have to), possibility (might / may / could); prohibition (mustn't) vs no obligation (don't have to)

pronunciation: Intonation — polite requests vs commands: rising, softer intonation for “Could you please...?” vs falling, firm intonation for “Kneel down and pray.”
pronunciation_detail: In English, the melody of a sentence can change its meaning completely. The same words can sound like a gentle request or a strict order — it all depends on your intonation. Vietnamese learners often use the same flat tone for both, so a polite request can sound like a command, and a command can sound weak. Learn the two melodies: Polite requests — RISING intonation (voice goes UP, softer and slower): “Could you please pray for my family?” — “Would you sing with us this morning?” — “Might I ask you to lead us in prayer?” The voice rises at the end, the words are soft, and the speaker often adds please. Use this melody when you ask someone for help, especially an older person or a guest. Commands — FALLING intonation (voice goes DOWN, firm and strong): “Kneel down and pray.” — “Bow down before the Lord!” — “Let us worship the Lord together.” The voice falls at the end, the words are firm and clear. Use this melody for commands in Scripture, for leading a group in worship, and for exhortations — never for asking a friend a favour. Watch out: if you say “Pray for my family” with falling intonation, it sounds like an order — and your friend may feel hurt. Add Could you please…? and let your voice rise, and the same request becomes kind. Practice: listen to the lesson audio and notice how the Friend says “Could you please pray with me now?” (rising, soft) and how the Narrator says “Let us bow down and pray together” (falling, firm). Shadow both lines, then read the pairs in Exercise 1 aloud with the correct melody.

grammar.title: Modals — advice (should / ought to), obligation (must / have to), possibility (might / may / could); prohibition (mustn't) vs no obligation (don't have to)
grammar.explain:
Modal verbs (should, ought to, must, have to, might, may, could) show the speaker's attitude: is this good advice, a duty, or only a possibility? The modal is always followed by the base verb (no -s, no to) — except ought to, which keeps its to. The form never changes for he / she / it: “He should pray”, not “He should prays”.

Structure 1: Advice — should / ought to (something is a good idea) “We should pray every day.” — “We ought to worship God with a sincere heart.” — “You should thank God for His goodness before you ask for more.” Ought to is a little stronger and more formal than should, and it is common in Bible teaching. Note the form: should + base verb but ought to + base verb. Never say “You should to pray” or “We ought worship”.

Structure 2: Obligation — must / have to (something is necessary) “True worshipers must worship the Father in spirit and truth.” (John 4:24) — “Christians have to gather together to worship God.” (Heb 10:25) Must is the speaker's own strong command — Jesus Himself uses it in John 4:24. Have to is an obligation that comes from outside — a rule, a situation, or someone else. In the negative they are very different: mustn't means “do not do it” (“We mustn't worship with a proud heart”), but don't have to means “it is not necessary” (“You don't have to pray for a long time — a short, sincere prayer is precious”).

Structure 3: Possibility & Permission — might / may / could “God might answer our prayer in a way we do not expect.” — “You may come to the prayer meeting tonight if you are free.” — “You could begin with a simple prayer.” Might shows a small possibility (less sure than may); may gives permission; could offers a gentle suggestion or a possibility. All three take the base verb: “God might answer”, not “God might answers”. Modal strength — from weakest to strongest: might / could (maybe) — may (permission / possibility) — should / ought to (good advice) — have to (necessary, from outside) — must (necessary, the speaker's command).

Watch out: never use to after should, must, might, may, could; only ought to and have to keep the to.

reading_passage: Psalm 95 begins with a joyful invitation: “Oh come, let us sing to the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation!” Then it gives the reason: the Lord is a great God and a great King above all gods. He made the sea and the dry land, and we are the people of His pasture, the sheep of His hand. So the psalm says, “Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker!” True worship begins with knowing who God is — and who we are. We should come to Him with a humble heart, because He is holy and we are small. We ought to thank Him for His goodness before we ask Him for anything. And we must remember that worship is not only singing; it is a whole life offered to God. In John 4, Jesus met a Samaritan woman at a well. She asked Him where people ought to worship — on the mountain or in Jerusalem. Jesus answered that true worshipers must worship the Father in spirit and truth. To worship in spirit means to worship with a sincere heart, not just with words or a ceremony. To worship in truth means to worship God as He really is, not as we imagine Him. The Father is seeking such people to worship Him. God might answer our prayers in a way we do not expect, but He always hears us. So we should pray every day, we ought to confess our sins honestly, and we must never worship with a proud heart. When we come to God in spirit and truth, we find what the woman at the well found: living water, and a Saviour who knows us completely and loves us still.

reading_comprehension.q: 1. According to Psalm 95, why should we worship the Lord?
reading_comprehension.a: Because the Lord is a great God and a great King, and He made us — He is our Maker.

reading_comprehension.q: 2. According to John 4:20, what did the Samaritan woman ask Jesus?
reading_comprehension.a: Where people ought to worship — on the mountain or in Jerusalem.

reading_comprehension.q: 3. According to John 4:24, how must those who worship God worship Him?
reading_comprehension.a: They must worship the Father in spirit and truth.

reading_comprehension.q: 4. According to John 4:23, whom is the Father seeking?
reading_comprehension.a: The Father is seeking such people to worship Him.

reading_comprehension.q: 5. According to John 4:25–26, what did the woman say, and how did Jesus answer?
reading_comprehension.a: The woman said, “I know that Messiah is coming,” and Jesus answered, “I who speak to you am He.”

listening_questions.q: 1. Where did Jesus meet the Samaritan woman?
2. What did the woman ask Jesus about?
listening_questions.a: Where people ought to worship — on the mountain or in Jerusalem.

listening_questions.q: 3. What did Jesus say true worshipers must do?
listening_questions.a: They must worship the Father in spirit and truth.

listening_questions.q: 4. What does “worship in spirit” mean, according to the narrator?
listening_questions.a: To worship with a sincere heart, not just with words.

listening_questions.q: 5. What might God do when we pray?
listening_questions.a: He might answer our prayer in a way we do not expect — but he always hears us.

listening_questions.q: 6. What did the Friend decide to do this week?
listening_questions.a: She decided to pray every morning this week, and to tell her sister about the living water.

exercises.title: Exercise 1: Intonation — Polite Requests or Commands?
exercises.instruction: Mark each sentence U (rising — voice goes UP: polite request) or D (falling — voice goes DOWN: command). Remember: polite requests with Could you...? / Would you...? rise; direct commands fall.

speaking_task: Roleplay in pairs (3 minutes): Student A is a new believer who wants to learn how to pray. Student B is a friend who helps. Student B gives advice with should and ought to (“You should pray every day”, “You ought to confess your sins honestly”), and talks about possibility with might and could (“God might answer in a way you do not expect”). Student A makes two polite requests with rising intonation (“Could you please pray with me?”) and gives one command with falling intonation (“Kneel down and pray with me.”). Use at least 5 vocabulary words from Section 3.
writing_task: Write a short prayer of worship (80-100 words) to God, beginning: “Lord, I come to worship You in spirit and truth...” Use at least 4 modal verbs (should / ought to / must / might / may / could) and 5 vocabulary words from Section 3. Include adoration, thanksgiving, and one request.

written: A. Rewrite these 5 sentences using a modal (should / ought to / must / might / may / could). 1) It is a good idea to pray every day. 2) It is necessary to worship God in spirit and truth. 3) It is possible that God will answer in a way we do not expect. 4) It is a good idea to confess our sins honestly. 5) You are allowed to come to the prayer meeting tonight.

B. Correct the mistake in each sentence (one mistake each). 1) We must to worship God with a humble heart. 2) You should to pray every day. 3) God might answers our prayer. 4) We ought worship in spirit and truth. 5) She mustn't to be proud when she prays.
C. Write 5 sentences about your own prayer life, using a different modal in each: should, ought to, must, might, could.
